title: Cloud / IaC / Supply Chain Advanced
description: Cloud identity, infrastructure-as-code, containers, and build pipelines.

attacks.name: Terraform state file
attacks.desc: A public Terraform state file can contain infrastructure addresses, resource attributes, and sensitive outputs.
attacks.prevention: Keep Terraform state in encrypted private storage with scoped access, versioning, and secret handling.

attacks.name: CloudFormation outputs
attacks.desc: Public CloudFormation outputs may expose service endpoints or resource identifiers.
attacks.prevention: Avoid exporting secrets from CloudFormation; restrict stack-output visibility to authorized operators.

attacks.name: IaC misconfig
attacks.desc: Infrastructure-as-code errors can deploy overly broad network access or public storage permissions.
attacks.prevention: Review IaC changes for public security groups, storage exposure, and broad roles before deployment.

attacks.name: Lambda env vars
attacks.desc: Exposed serverless environment variables can contain credentials or internal service configuration.
attacks.prevention: Limit access to Lambda configuration, avoid long-lived secrets in environment variables, and use a secret manager.

attacks.name: Lambda event injection
attacks.desc: Untrusted event fields may reach dangerous operations inside a serverless function without validation.
attacks.prevention: Validate event schemas and never interpret event fields as commands or expressions.

attacks.name: Cloud IAM role confusion
attacks.desc: A confused-deputy IAM relationship can let another principal use privileges outside the intended trust scope.
attacks.prevention: Set explicit IAM trust conditions and external IDs where applicable, and restrict who can assume privileged roles.

attacks.name: S3 ACL vs policy mismatch
attacks.desc: Conflicting bucket ACL and policy settings can produce unexpected access to S3 objects.
attacks.prevention: Audit bucket ACLs and policies together, block public access by default, and test effective permissions.

attacks.name: CloudFront origin leak
attacks.desc: Origin details leaked outside CloudFront can make direct-to-origin traffic possible if network rules allow it.

attacks.name: Container registry exposure
attacks.desc: A public container registry may expose images containing application code, dependencies, or secrets.

attacks.name: Docker socket mount
attacks.desc: A container with access to the host Docker socket can control the daemon and potentially the host.

attacks.name: K8s API anonymous
attacks.desc: An anonymous Kubernetes API endpoint can expose cluster resources or operations if authorization is weak.

attacks.name: K8s RBAC misconfig
attacks.desc: Overly broad Kubernetes service-account permissions can let one workload access unrelated resources.

attacks.name: Helm/Tiller exposure
attacks.desc: Legacy Helm/Tiller exposure can grant extensive cluster operations to an unauthorized client.

attacks.name: CI secret leakage
attacks.desc: Build logs can reveal credentials or tokens if secret values are printed during CI jobs.

attacks.name: Dependency confusion
attacks.desc: A public package with a private dependency's name can be selected by an unsafe package-resolution setup.

attacks.name: Typosquat package
attacks.desc: A lookalike package name can trick a maintainer into installing attacker-controlled code.

attacks.name: Lockfile tampering
attacks.desc: Changing a lockfile can pin a project to a malicious or unintended dependency version.

attacks.name: Post-install script RCE
attacks.desc: Package lifecycle hooks can execute code during installation when a dependency is untrusted.

attacks.name: GitHub Actions injection
attacks.desc: Untrusted workflow event text can become shell commands when inserted directly into a GitHub Actions run step.

attacks.name: Artifact poisoning
attacks.desc: Replacing a CI artifact can make later jobs deploy or execute content that was not produced by the trusted build.
